entry: Japanese animation studio based in Koganei, Tokyo. Founded on June 15, 1985, by directors [[Hayao Miyazaki]] and Isao Takahata and producer Toshio Suzuki, it is known for hand-drawn [[Animation|animated]] features. Its mascot, Totoro, comes from *My Neighbor Totoro* (1988). Its highest-grossing films include *Princess Mononoke* (1997), *Spirited Away* (2001), and *Howl's Moving Castle* (2004). The studio has won two Academy Awards for Best Animated Feature.

Method of filmmaking in which a small number of large studios dominated film production and distribution. The term most often refers to Hollywood from 1927, when sound films were introduced, to 1948, when the system began to end. Studios produced films on their own lots, used long-term contracts for actors and filmmaking personnel, and controlled exhibition through vertical integration, including ownership of theaters. The original Big Five were [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer]], [[Paramount Pictures]], Warner Bros., 20th Century-Fox, and RKO Radio Pictures, while [[Columbia Pictures]] and [[Universal Pictures]] were organized similarly on a smaller scale. A 1948 Supreme Court antitrust ruling sought to separate production from distribution and exhibition. By 1954, with [[Television|television]] competing for audiences, the historic era of the studio system was over.

[[Toy|Toy]] made of fabric sewn around a soft, flexible stuffing, most often shaped like an animal. Also called plush toys, plushies, or teddies, stuffed toys are commonly made of plush fabric and synthetic fiber. In the late 19th century, Margarete Steiff and the Steiff company of Germany created the first stuffed animals. In 1902, a political cartoon of [[Theodore Roosevelt]] inspired the "Teddy's bear." In 1921, A. A. Milne gave a stuffed bear to his son, which inspired [[Winnie-the-Pooh]]. In the 1990s, Ty Warner's Beanie Babies, animals stuffed with plastic pellets, became popular collector's items. Early toys used felt, velvet, or mohair stuffed with straw or sawdust, while modern ones use cotton, synthetic fiber, or beans. Since 2005, toys-to-life stuffed toys have been used to access digital content in video games and online worlds.

Ray-finned fish of the family Acipenseridae, comprising 27 species. Sturgeons are native to subtropical, temperate, and sub-Arctic rivers, lakes, and coastlines of [[Eurasia]] and [[North America]]. They are long-lived, late-maturing fish with a heterocercal tail similar to that of [[Shark|sharks]] and smooth, scaleless bodies armored with five rows of bony plates called scutes. Several species typically range 2–3.5 m (7–12 ft) in length. The largest sturgeon on record, a beluga female captured in the [[Volga]] Delta in 1827, measured 7.2 m (23 ft 7 in) and weighed 1,571 kg (3,463 lb). Most species are anadromous bottom-feeders that spawn upstream and feed in river deltas and estuaries. Their roe is processed into caviar, and overexploitation has brought most species to critically endangered status.

Capital and largest city of the German state of [[Baden-Württemberg]] (pop., 2023: 613,111). Stuttgart lies on the Neckar River in a fertile valley and is known as the "cradle of the automobile." Its museums include the [[Mercedes-Benz]] Museum and the Porsche Museum, and it is home to the headquarters of Porsche, Bosch, and Mercedes-Benz Group. Its stock exchange is the second largest in Germany, after [[Frankfurt]]. Founded in the tenth century as a stud farm for warhorses, the town was granted a charter in 1320 and was the capital of the House of Württemberg's county, duchy, and kingdom from the 15th century to 1918. Badly damaged by air raids in [[World War II|World War II]], it had become a major cultural and industrial center by 1952. The city hosted matches in the 1974 and 2006 FIFA World Cups.

Chinese poet, prose writer, and scholar-official of the [[Song dynasty]]. In 1057 he and his younger brother, Su Zhe, passed the highest-level civil service examinations, and the literary figure [[Ouyang Xiu]] became his patron. His prose, ranging from philosophical to culinary, earned him a place among the Eight Masters of the Tang and Song, and he is counted among the Four Masters of Song Calligraphy. As a painter he was known for bamboo and weathered rocks. He held posts across China, most notably in [[Hangzhou]], where he built a causeway across the [[West Lake]]. Caught in factional struggles at court, he spent much of his career in exile, and his literary output flourished during these periods.

Chinese [[Polymath|polymathic]] scientist and statesman of the [[Song dynasty]]. He excelled in [[Mathematics|mathematics]], astronomy, cartography, [[Metallurgy|metallurgy]], and [[Mechanical engineering|mechanical engineering]]. He engineered a hydro-mechanical astronomical clock tower in Kaifeng that used an early escapement mechanism and 133 clock jacks to indicate and sound the hours. He described it in the treatise *Xinyi Xiangfayao*, written in 1092 and printed in 1094. The clock was dismantled and moved north to Beijing in 1127, and the tower was never successfully reinstated. He also compiled a celestial atlas, terrestrial maps, and a treatise on pharmacology covering mineralogy, zoology, botany, and metallurgy. In 1077 he was sent on a diplomatic mission to the [[Liao dynasty]], where he admitted that the Khitan calendar was a bit more accurate than the Song calendar.

Group within a larger culture that differentiates itself from the values of the mainstream. Subcultures develop their own norms and values regarding cultural, political, and sexual matters, yet coexist with mainstream society while keeping their characteristics intact. The concept was developed in [[Sociology|sociology]] and cultural studies from the 1940s–1950s, primarily in North America and the United Kingdom. Examples include punks, [[Skinhead|skinheads]], Teddy Boys, mods, rockers, bikers, and hip-hoppers. In his 1979 book *Subculture: The Meaning of Style*, Dick Hebdige argued that subcultures are a subversion of normalcy and can be perceived as negative. In 1995, Sarah Thornton, drawing on [[Pierre Bourdieu]], described "subcultural capital" as the cultural knowledge and commodities that raise a member's status. Subcultures differ from countercultures.

Indian anti-colonial nationalist, honored as Netaji ("Respected Leader"). Born into wealth in a large Bengali family, Bose joined the movement led by [[Mahatma Gandhi]] after returning to India in 1921. He became president of the [[Indian National Congress]] in 1938, but after his reelection in 1939, disputes over strategy and non-violence led to his resignation. In 1941 he went to [[Nazi Germany]], where he recruited a 3,000-strong Free India Legion from Indian prisoners of war, and in 1942 he met [[Adolf Hitler]]. He then moved to Japanese-held Southeast Asia and revived the Indian National Army. Bose died of third-degree burns after a plane crash in [[Taiwan]], then under Japanese occupation. He is admired in India as a hero, but his collaboration with Japanese fascism and Nazism poses serious ethical dilemmas.

Magazine-fed automatic carbine designed to fire handgun cartridges. John T. Thompson coined the term to describe a weapon with less firepower than a [[Machine gun|machine gun]]. Developed during [[World War I]] as a close-quarter weapon for trench raiding, submachine guns were produced in the millions during [[World War II]]. [[Cold War|Cold War]] designs appeared frequently, especially among special forces and commandos. Frontline combat use declined in the 1980s and 1990s. Personal defense weapons such as the FN P90 are a subset of the category.

Watercraft capable of independent operation underwater. Unlike submersibles, which have more limited underwater capability, submarines are called boats regardless of size. Submarine design advanced in the 19th century, and submarines were first used widely in [[World War I|World War I]]; many [[Navy|navies]] operate them today. Military uses include attacking enemy ships, protecting [[Aircraft carrier|aircraft carriers]], blockade running, nuclear deterrence, and stealth reconnaissance. Civilian uses include marine science, salvage, exploration, and facility inspection. Submarines dive by changing the amount of water and air in ballast tanks, which alters their [[Buoyancy|buoyancy]]. Sizes range from one- or two-person craft that operate for a few hours to the Russian Typhoon class, the largest submarines ever built, which can remain submerged for six months. More countries now build and operate submarines than ever before, with China leading the construction surge.

Set whose elements are all members of another set. Written A ⊆ B, the relation is called inclusion, and B is then a superset of A. If the sets are unequal, A is a proper subset of B, written A ⊊ B. The empty set is a subset of every set, and every set is a subset of itself. The set {1, 2} is a proper subset of {1, 2, 3}. The [[Natural number|natural numbers]] are a proper subset of the [[Rational number|rational numbers]], which are a proper subset of the [[Real number|real numbers]]; the latter has greater [[Cardinality|cardinality]]. The set of all subsets of a set is its power set, which inclusion partially orders.

Government expenditure that redistributes money from taxpayers to individuals, households, or businesses. Subsidies take forms such as direct cash grants, interest-free loans, tax breaks, price supports, and government provision of goods and services. Production subsidies, which offset producers' costs to expand output, are critically discussed for causing problems such as the cost of storing surplus goods, depressed world market prices, and overproduction. Consumption subsidies lower what buyers pay; some governments offer "lifeline" electricity rates, subsidizing the first increment of each month's use. Among [[OECD]] countries in 2020, subsidies and other transfers had a median value of 56.3 percent of total government expenses.

Farming on smallholdings to meet the needs of a farmer's own family. Planting decisions are made principally for what the family will need in the coming year, and only secondarily for market prices. Most subsistence farmers still trade, mainly to obtain goods such as sugar or bicycles rather than food. The system typically features small capital requirements, mixed cropping, limited use of [[Fertilizer|fertilizer]] and [[Pesticide|pesticides]], traditional tools, and low yields. It was the dominant mode of production in Europe and North America until around 1800 and had largely disappeared from Europe by the beginning of the 20th century. In 2015, about 2 billion people, slightly more than 25% of the world's population, lived as smallholder farmers, working less than 2 [[Hectare|hectares]] (5 acres) of land.

Need for a drug, the discontinuation of which produces withdrawal symptoms. Also called drug dependence, it is a biopsychological condition in which a person's functioning depends on repeated consumption of a psychoactive substance. Withdrawal, the body's reaction to abstinence, can involve physical symptoms, emotional and motivational symptoms, or both, and it promotes continued use. Dependence potential varies by substance and individual, and dose, frequency, [[Pharmacokinetics|pharmacokinetics]], route of administration, and time are critical factors. Psychological dependence involves gene-expression changes in the nucleus accumbens, where dynorphin reduces [[Dopamine|dopamine]] release. Unlike [[Addiction|addiction]], which is compulsive use despite negative consequences, physical dependence can occur without it. The DSM-5 (2013) merged substance abuse and substance dependence into [[Substance use disorder|substance use disorders]].

Persistent use of [[Drug|drugs]] despite substantial harm and adverse consequences to self and others. Symptoms include chronic guilt, an inability to reduce or stop use despite repeated attempts, operating vehicles while intoxicated, and physiological withdrawal. Commonly involved drug classes include [[Alcoholism|alcohol]], cannabis, [[Opioid|opioids]], and stimulants such as [[Nicotine]] and [[Cocaine]]. The DSM-5 (2013) merged substance abuse and substance dependence into this category, rating severity as mild, moderate, or severe by the number of 11 criteria met. Co-occurring [[Mental disorder|mental health disorders]] are common. Effects on the body include liver failure, [[Hypertension|hypertension]], kidney failure, and transmission of [[HIV]] through shared needles. In 2017, substance use disorders from illicit substances directly caused 585,000 deaths, and alcohol use caused an additional 3 million deaths in 2016.

Chemical reaction in which one functional group in a compound is replaced by another. Also called single displacement or single substitution, it is of prime importance in [[Organic chemistry|organic chemistry]], where reactions are classified as electrophilic or nucleophilic depending on the reagent. In nucleophilic substitution, a nucleophile attacks a substrate and displaces a leaving group. The SN1 mechanism proceeds in two steps through a carbocation and usually causes racemization, while the one-step SN2 mechanism always results in inversion of configuration. A classic example is halogenation: when [[Chlorine]] gas (Cl₂) is irradiated, its molecules split into [[Radical (chemistry)|radicals]] that form hydrogen chloride and methyl chloride (CH₃Cl) from methane (CH₄). Understanding the reaction type helps predict products and optimize conditions such as temperature and solvent.

Arithmetic operation, signified by the minus sign (−), that represents the removal of objects from a collection. For example, 5 − 2 = 3. Subtraction is the inverse of [[Addition|addition]]: c − b = a if and only if c + b = a. It is anti-commutative, changing the sign of the result when the order is reversed, and it is not associative. While primarily associated with [[Natural number|natural numbers]], subtraction also applies to [[Negative number|negative numbers]], [[Fraction|fractions]], [[Irrational number|irrational numbers]], and vectors. In computability theory, subtraction on natural numbers is defined as truncated subtraction, or monus. The English word comes from the Latin *subtrahere*, meaning to draw from below.

Predominantly residential area within a [[Metropolitan area|metropolitan area]], within commuting distance of a large city. Suburbs may have their own political jurisdictions, especially in the United States, but in the [[United Kingdom]] most are within city boundaries. Suburbs emerged on a large scale in the 19th and 20th centuries as improved rail and road transport increased commuting. Most are less dense than inner-city neighborhoods. In Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa, suburbs are formal geographic subdivisions of a city used in postal addressing, and the terms inner and outer suburb distinguish higher-density areas near the center from outlying ones. In the United States, areas beyond the suburbs are called exurbs. Although most Americans regard themselves as suburban residents, the federal government has no formal definition of a suburb.

Mongol general and the primary military strategist of [[Genghis Khan]] and [[Ögedei Khan]]. He directed more than 20 campaigns and conquered more territory than any other commander in history, as part of the expansion of the [[Mongol Empire]]. He often won through sophisticated strategies, coordinating armies that operated hundreds of kilometers apart. A commoner by birth, he joined Temujin's army at 14 and became a general within a decade. In the invasion of northern China in 1211 he was partnered with the senior general Jebe. Under Ögedei he directed the western campaign with [[Batu Khan]], subjugating the Rus' principalities and invading [[Poland|Poland]], Hungary, and Bulgaria. He is regarded as one of the greatest military commanders in history and the greatest in Mongolian history.

Female [[Demon|demon]] in European folklore who appears in men's dreams to seduce them. Repeated encounters lead to sexual activity and can produce a hybrid child called a cambion, at the expense of the man's health, which may eventually lead to his death. The male counterpart is the [[Incubus|incubus]]. Folkloric belief was often motivated by nighttime phenomena, chiefly wet dreams and [[Sleep paralysis|sleep paralysis]]. In *Malleus Maleficarum* (Witches' Hammer), written in 1486, succubi were said to collect semen that incubi used to father children. Legendary magician [[Merlin]] was said to have been fathered by an incubus.

Disaccharide composed of glucose and fructose subunits, with the formula C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁. Also called saccharose, it occurs naturally in plants and is the main constituent of white [[Sugar|sugar]]. For human consumption it is refined from [[Sugarcane|sugarcane]] or [[Sugar beet|sugar beet]]. The name sucrose was coined in 1857 by the English chemist William Miller. Digestion splits it into glucose and fructose. About 185 million [[Tonne|tonnes]] of sugar were produced worldwide in 2017.

Country in northeastern Africa, the third-largest in Africa by area (pop., 2025: 51.8 million). The capital and largest city is [[Khartoum]]. The area was home to the [[Kingdom of Kush]] (c. 785 BC–350 AD) and later Nubian Christian kingdoms, and Arab nomads settled most of the country between the 14th and 15th centuries. Egyptian forces under the Muhammad Ali dynasty conquered all of Sudan in the 19th century. In 1899 Egypt agreed to share sovereignty with the United Kingdom as a condominium, in effect making Sudan a British possession. Sudan became independent on January 1, 1956. The secession of [[South Sudan]] in 2011 followed a second civil war. From 1989 to 2019 a military dictatorship led by Omar al-Bashir ruled the country, which ranked 170th on the [[Human Development Index]] in 2024.

Civil war in [[Sudan]] between the army-led government of General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by General Hemedti. Fighting began on April 15, 2023, after a power struggle within the transitional administration. As of July 6, 2026, the conflict had displaced over 14 million people, including 4.5 million refugees. The RSF took El Fasher on October 26, 2025; one estimate puts the deaths there at 60,000 to 70,000. On January 7, 2025, the U.S. government formally determined that the RSF committed genocide.

Logic-based, combinatorial number-placement [[Puzzle|puzzle]] using a 9×9 grid. The grid is divided into nine 3×3 boxes, and the goal is to fill every row, column, and box with the digits 1 to 9. A well-posed puzzle has a single solution. Its modern form was first published in 1979 by Dell Magazines as *Number Place*, most likely designed by Howard Garns. Japanese publisher Nikoli popularized it in 1984 and shortened the name to sudoku in 1986. In 2004 it appeared in newspapers outside Japan, including *The Times* of London.
